source.title: With Greater Distance Comes Worse Performance: On the Perspective of Layer Utilization and Model Generalization

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether final-layer weight utilization tracks generalization and its proposed effective-complexity account, using a different measure and setup from the original double-descent studies.
record.gate_note: The study reports model-size/noise-ratio heatmaps for generalization gap and resilience, but these are not direct measurements of the test-error curve named in V1 or of changing training-sample count as named in V3. Those results are recorded under fits_no_version. It explicitly excludes epoch-wise double descent from its experiments. Its direct utilization-versus-generalization comparison bears on V5.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the double-descent and effective-model-complexity framing to motivate its own proxy: final-layer weight distance from initialization. It reports how well that proxy tracks a train–test loss gap. It never reports test error against model size, epochs or sample count. It does not test whether a single complexity measure predicts where the test-error peak falls. Its model-size × noise-ratio heatmaps measure the generalization gap and a 'resilience' risk, both constructs related to but different from the test-error curve the versions name. All of these results therefore go under fits_no_version, not verdicts.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. One qualification: the support for reinitializing final layers to revert overfit rests on the negative contribution of deeper layers to testing loss and resilience (Fig. 5). No accuracy comparison before and after reinitialization is reported. The interpolation-threshold patterns are in the generalization gap and resilience, not in test error.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies fully connected network hidden-layer size and label-noise ratio on MNIST and CIFAR10, rather than varying training-sample count as in the cited double-descent work; it evaluates generalization gap and resilience and trains models for 10000 epochs.
record.method_sensitivity: The interpolation-threshold pattern shifts with hidden-layer size and label-noise ratio; resilience has a more obscure second descent and is notably worse in the large-hidden-layer, low-noise region.

fits_no_version.finding: In deeper layers, final-layer utilization (L2 distance of weights from initialization) is positively correlated with the train–test loss gap and with resilience. This is shown in figures only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deeper-layer weight distance from initialization tracks the generalization gap in fully connected networks across model size and label-noise ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: The maximum of the generalization gap traces a diagonal across hidden-layer size and label-noise ratio. The authors read this as an interpolation threshold that shifts with data complexity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The peak of the train–test gap shifts to larger models as label-noise ratio rises, analogous to the model-wise interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Resilience shows the same diagonal pattern, but its second descent is much more obscure. It is worse for large models trained on low-noise data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Risk on recovered labels after noisy-label training shows a weak double-descent pattern over model size.

record.problems: Experiments are limited to fully connected networks on MNIST and CIFAR10. Exact plotted values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text. The authors note that test-loss convergence can be asynchronous, making generalization measurements uncertain.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over model size; only the train–test loss gap is reported.
Epoch-wise double descent is explicitly excluded; models are trained 10000 epochs.
Sample count is not varied; label-noise ratio is used as a data-complexity knob instead.
Only fully connected networks are used.
There is no test of whether a complexity measure predicts the test-error peak location along size, epoch or sample axes. The utilization proxy is only correlated with the generalization gap.
Noise ratio is varied, but the study does not test whether the test-error peak is noise-driven, splits into several peaks, or vanishes under tuned regularization.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked r1/r2 to V5 and labelled V5 'supports'. That link is dropped here: the study validates its own proxy against the train–test gap rather than testing EMC's prediction of the test-error peak. All evidence is figure-only, with no numerical correlations or uncertainty. Runs: 3 on MNIST, 6 on CIFAR10.

versions.untested_parts: No direct test-error curve over model size is reported; the study's double-descent heatmap uses a train-test generalization gap.
Epoch-wise double descent is explicitly outside the study's focus; models are trained for 10000 epochs before inference.
The study varies label-noise ratio, not the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
Experiments use fully connected neural networks only and do not test general double descent across model classes.
The study relates final-layer utilization to generalization in model-size and label-noise/data-complexity settings, but does not test prediction of peak location along the sample-count or epoch axes.
Label-noise ratios are varied, but the study does not test whether noise drives the peak, multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
The study does not test whether measuring against an effective number of parameters converts second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
